title: Dr. Katherine Roche:
format: 16:9 only · 1920×1080 (client asked for longer researcher versions; same look as the approved short)
headline: A basic scientist who likes people: how the GRIN families moved her lab to patient variants, and the NIH research hospital study that now lets families take part.
story: The film opens on the person, not the credential: “I'm kind of a people person.” Then her name, and a title card with the music landing: A research hospital where no one pays.

Dr. Roche worked on glutamate receptors for 30 years. When genetics found patient variants in the proteins she studied, her lab pivoted to them. The GRIN community changed her research. Drugs may be further along than you would think, but science is slow, and gene correction is further out.
After a short break, the NIH study: patients can now come to the NIH clinical center under a research protocol. It is not a normal hospital; it is a research hospital. It ends on why: the families.
do: Open on her human moment with the hook text on frame 1, then a 3-shot B-roll button, then her name.
Let the music land on the title card. Break the film in the middle with the chapter card and a music change.
Two short AI-voiced explainers with text, where the science gets dense (glutamate receptors, cell lines).
Keep bites 6a and 6b together. Keep her limits on the study (“It's not a normal hospital … under a protocol”).
Frame tighter than the camera did, and improve the bare background with AI (window, flowers or a painting).
dont: Don't open on “small progress is important” (the short's hook).
No free-care or sign-up framing. No address, phone or “how to sign up”.
Don't tell the other researchers' stories (Traynelis, Park, Penn). No shot the other researcher films use.
No stock footage. No frames where the camera hunts for the next shot.

voice.quote: so I am a basic researcher. And I got my PhD a very long time ago. And I've been working on glutamate receptors really the entire time. … But then there was this explosion in human genetics where more and more patient populations were getting sequenced. And it became clear that sometimes there were mutations, single point mutations, in individuals that caused a lot of problems. They were pathogenic. And it turned out that some of these variants are in the proteins I had studied for decades.

voice.quote: And I started off being a very basic scientist and really have pivoted. Our lab almost entirely focuses our research on these rare variants that are found in patient populations. So we primarily study NMDA receptors. And they're encoded by the GRIN genes, in particular GRIN2B and GRIN2A.

voice.quote: Half my lab studies one class of proteins, which has been known for decades, even before the genetics, the next-gen sequencing, caught up to be important. But there's no advocacy group. voice.quote: That's all changed in the last few months. I'm now associated with the neurogenetics team at NINDS. And this is really fabulous for me and I think for the research and the people that are affected, hopefully, by my research in that we can bring in patients to the clinical center. You would have to get to Bethesda and you'd obviously have to schedule it and all that. But we could collect all the clinical data. The clinicians can take blood samples. They can take skin biopsy. These are important if we want to make cell lines, patient-derived cell lines.

voice.quote: So NIH has the largest clinical research hospital in the world. No one pays. They don't even have a billing department. So you would have to get to Bethesda. But if you're brought in under this protocol, which is a very broad protocol looking at genetic disorders, then you could get these analyses. And you could contribute the information and blood samples. And it would all be taken care of. It's not a normal hospital. You wouldn't go to the clinical center if you broke your leg or if you're having a baby. It's a research hospital. So almost every patient that's certainly an inpatient, and even these, you have to be under a protocol. So it's all research associated.
